# fang

> Fang is a Python-embedded language for circuit boards and the typed kernel that holds what you write. You author intent: typed interfaces, parameters carrying units and constraints. The kernel elaborates that into one canonical model, refuses anything it cannot justify and lowers what survives into netlists, views, simulation decks and KiCad.

The five rules that explain most of fang's behaviour, and the
mistakes to avoid when answering questions about it:

1. One canonical model. There is exactly one persisted representation of a
   design, the Engineering Intermediate Representation. A netlist, a view, a
   SPICE deck and a KiCad file are lowerings, projections or interchange
   encodings of it, never second stores. Constructing a second constraint
   registry raises ELAB-0012.
2. Undecided is a third truth value. An unknown operand makes a check
   undecided, never a quiet pass and never a quiet failure. Whether undecided
   blocks a commit is the gate's policy decision, not the evaluator's.
3. Unknown is a status, not a null. Value.unknown() is distinct from absent, and
   sources that disagree stay unresolved as a ConflictingValue.
4. Pin assignment is a lowering result, never an authoring input. Programs
   connect typed interfaces; the kernel decides which pads carry them and
   records a decision naming the alternatives it rejected.
5. Nothing is invented to fill a gap. A missing simulator reports unsupported, a
   missing model rejects the plan, an unrepresentable CAD construct is named in
   the import report and a generic part carries no manufacturer until one is
   selected.

Two things that are commonly got wrong. The PyPI distribution is
"copperhead-fang", not "fang", though the import name is fang. And the third
truth value is spelled Truth.UNDECIDED, while the check status for the same idea
is CheckStatus.UNKNOWN.

The full text of every page below is available in one file at
https://fang.copperhead.sh/llms-full.txt.

## Concepts

- [Three phases](https://fang.copperhead.sh/concepts/three-phases/): Why elaboration, operation and commit happen in that order.
- [One canonical model](https://fang.copperhead.sh/concepts/one-canonical-model/): The governing invariant and what it costs to hold.
- [Values and undecided](https://fang.copperhead.sh/concepts/values-and-undecided/): How the kernel represents a value it does not know, and a constraint it cannot decide.
- [The commit gate](https://fang.copperhead.sh/concepts/the-commit-gate/): The six conditions every change passes before it reaches canonical state.
- [Interfaces and lowering](https://fang.copperhead.sh/concepts/interfaces-and-lowering/): How a typed connection lowers to pins, and what that decides.
- [Rationale](https://fang.copperhead.sh/concepts/rationale/): Why a value is what it is, as entities rather than prose.

## Examples

- [divider](https://fang.copperhead.sh/examples/divider/): A voltage divider with a capacitor across its output: two resistors, one cap, and nothing else. It is here to show the shape of a Fang program and no more than…
- [blinky](https://fang.copperhead.sh/examples/blinky/): An MCU pin, a series resistor, and an LED: the board everybody builds first. Read it after divider/, because it is the first example where the parts have…
- [sensor_board](https://fang.copperhead.sh/examples/sensor_board/): A regulated board with an MCU and an I2C sensor on it. This is the example to read to understand lowering: what happens between a typed interface and the pads…
- [equations](https://fang.copperhead.sh/examples/equations/): A divider written as the ratio it has to satisfy, rather than as two numbers someone computed offstage — and then reused, by inheritance, at a different ratio.
- [i2c_bus](https://fang.copperhead.sh/examples/i2c_bus/): One controller and three targets on a shared I2C bus. A bus is multi-drop, so the same port is connected three times and the lowering resolves it into one net…
- [buck_regulator](https://fang.copperhead.sh/examples/buck_regulator/): 12 V to 3.3 V, with the reasoning kept beside the circuit. The converter itself is ordinary; what is not ordinary is that the argument for it is in the same…
- [usb_uart_bridge](https://fang.copperhead.sh/examples/usb_uart_bridge/): USB to serial: the interface board on nearly every desk. What it adds over the other examples is part selection — the difference between what the design needs…
- [servo_drive](https://fang.copperhead.sh/examples/servo_drive/): Three half-bridges, CAN, an encoder and a shunt per phase: the board this toolchain was written for. It is the composition example — the largest program here,…

## Source of truth

The normative document is the specification at
https://github.com/copperheadhq/fang/blob/main/openspec/specs/fang-kernel/spec.md.
Where these pages and the spec disagree, the spec is right. The source is at
https://github.com/copperheadhq/fang.
